tone_statements.citation: Knop, G. 1954. De spraakkunst der Terschellinger dialecten. Taalkundige Bijdragen van Noord en Zuid VI. Assen: Van Gorcum. XXVI+270 pp. (ed. J.H. Brouwer, posthumous).
tone_statements.quote: Opm. Oudere Terschellingers maken verschil tussen a: in [hs:t] hard en de tweetoppige vocaal a: in [hs<:'t] haard. Ook s<:>t enz. werden tweetoppig gesproken, zodat men tweemaal a hoorde: [5/<D>t]. [...] < > boven vocaal duidt tweetoppig accent aan. [...] § 381. In tegenstelling tot het ndl., waarin de oppositie lang-kort een concomitant verschijnsel is bij de oppositie gedekt-ongedektis de lang-kort-correlatie in 't fri.-tersch. primair. [Delpher scanned verbatim; bracketed phonetic forms are scanned-garbled: hs:t = ha:t, hs<:'t = hâ:t, s<:>t = â:t 'oud']
tone_statements.translation: Note. Older Terschellingers make a difference between a: in [ha:t] 'hard' and the two-peaked vowel â: in [hâ:t] 'haard' (hearth). Also â:t ('oud') etc. were spoken two-peaked, so that one heard a twice. [...] ^ over a vowel marks two-peaked accent. [...] § 381. In contrast to Dutch, in which the long-short opposition is a concomitant of the checked-free opposition, in Terschelling Frisian the long-short correlation is primary.
tone_statements.locator: ch. I Klankleer A.1, § 7 Opm., p. 3, continuation ('Ook.. werden tweetoppig gesproken..') top of p. 4 before § 8; phonetic-symbol list in the front matter; ch. III.A § 381 p. 122; ADD ch. III.A § 397 (c. p. 127): phonemic status of plain vs two-peaked long open-o

tone.quote: Een overeenkomst tussen de Waddendialecten waar men in de literatuur vaker op heeft gewezen, is die in de uitspraak. Men zou op de eilanden wat zangeriger spreken dan elders. Dit kenmerk wordt ook wel voor andere kustdialecten genoemd.
tone.locator: ch. 1, section 'Spreken tegen de wind in', p. 7 of the KNAW author version; Westers vowel list 'Wyt, wiid, wiet' starts p. 28
tone.translation: A similarity between the Wadden dialects that has been pointed out repeatedly in the literature lies in pronunciation. People on the islands are said to speak somewhat more sing-song than elsewhere. This feature is also mentioned for other coastal dialects.
